blocks.x: Yeah, what's your name? Clayton Dure. How do you spell it? D-U-E-R-R. And let's see, what's the day? The day is April the, you know the day? 17th. April 17th. Yeah, and where are we at 4,400? Hollygrove. Hollygrove, yeah. My name is Dick Allen. What's your name? Laura Cittagone. Okay. You want to tell us about where you were born and when? Well, I was born in New Orleans down
to French Quarter until I was about 13 years old and we moved out to this place here. And I didn't start to play fool around with a banjo until I was about 15, I guess.

That way we'll know. First track. Yeah, what were you gonna say? We're talking about the French Quarter and going back there and the houses. I wanted to ask you some more about Carnival. Did they have any bands and music at Carnival? Any brass bands or anything?

Well there was bands years ago. I guess there's always been music in Carnival and so on that course. I grew up in the Quarter. I remember certain things about Carnival, like I said it was a little different than it is now because the Quarter was not the same as it is now. But as kids I mean we used to mask and stay around the middle. Then when I went away, I mean I was away for ten years and when I came back I was about different then. New Orleans was different when you came back? Well not so much when I came back in 1936. It changed since then. It wasn't too much change when I came back. I was having to live in New York ten years and I felt like I was coming back to the whole country town. When I came back here, you spend ten years in a big city like New York and you come back here, it really feels funny. You liked it better in New York? I liked it at the time but I wouldn't like it now at the time. No, no. It was all new and all the glamour and all the bright lights and all and all those things. I got a kick out of being up there. Then you didn't want to go back there again? No. Who was the first? I'd like to go back for a visit, you know what I mean. I'd take a trip up there sometime. I might do that someday. Take a look around and see.
You've been living in this address here since 1936?
No, I've been living here since 1921 or something like that. 20 or 21 I think.
Then you moved to New York for the point. What do you think the changes have been here in this section?

Oh, but when we came out here, there was no sewage out here, nothing. There was just mud streets. This was like really in the country. It was like the country. Yeah. You see, my father used to come out, he knew some people who had a truck form over here, just around the corner on Hamilton Street. He knew these people, I guess his people must have known these people, they were from Germany too. They owned about two squares of ground over here on Hamilton Street. They sold it all to the country for a little while, you know what I mean, caught their families off, couldn't have gone. I mean, they were all over here somewhere.
So when you were moved out here, you were the only house right here?

No, no, this house was over here. There was a few houses. This house, they had an old house over there. This knocked us down, here's the staff put a brick house up there. There was an old house there, it was there, and this other house back in here was here. It wasn't too many, it wasn't built up down the street like it is there. Yeah. But there was some houses, there were people out here, but there wasn't.
There wasn't too many roads.

No, they didn't, like I said, they didn't have much sidewalks either. No. I remember the people that owned this farm over there, we used to buy milk from them, we used to go over the evening and get a picture of milk. They had cows and all, you know what I mean, you get a picture of milk from them. Did they have schools in this neighborhood there? Well, when I moved out here, I was going, I started high school.
Yeah, how did you get to school from here? It would have been a long way.
I used to walk to Canal Street and take the streetcars, and then they had the Napoleon, the Napoleon cars used to come along here.
I see.

They used to come out on Napoleon Avenue, come on the Calton and then come around here, and then they used to go all the way to Shrewsbury. There used to be a line that used to go all the way along here. There were all streetcars in that time. All the way out to Shrewsbury. I see. And then, but I used to-
Was that a kick to go out to Shrewsbury then?

Yeah, it was. It was like the Spanish Fortress used to be a big deal. In those days, when they had the streetcars that made it to trains like, they used to come on Canal Street by Rampart there. And then on a Saturday, Saturday people used to, there was calls used to fill up one behind, they'd hook about three or four calls together. And they'd leave every few minutes and they'd be jammed up people hanging on the outside going out to the way. But the big deal was about the Spanish Fort that they used to call the Spanish Fort out there.
Yeah. This was all white here then? Hmm? This was all white neighborhood here? It was, no, there was some color back there.

There's always been colored back there. Yeah. But it was mostly white, there was a lot of white people back there. Yeah. You know, you take all over towards, a little bit further over to Monroe Street there, there was always a few colors.
I noticed when I came up on the back from that way, it was all colored all the way up there.
Oh, it's all colored now, yeah. It's all colored. Sure, when I worked in Sean for a 15 and a half machine, you know, and my debit was from right in here, back up to Claymore.
Yeah.

And you sold the white for Shane? I used to have some cases in here between here and the airline highway going back to this. You see, I used to go back, walk back, Harley goes to the airline highway back there, across the airline highway, Bahamut and Street. And I used to pick up a few collections in here, you know, some white families have insurance in here, but gradually they all left for the camera. I've been retired from Shane for three years, you know, almost three years. And towards the end there, there was just a couple of people that I used to collect from, you know.
Well what was in Shrewsbury then?

It wasn't nothing in Shrewsbury. I don't know how. It was just the end of the line. It was just the end of the line. It was just the end of the line. I see, I just wanted to have some homes and stuff where people would go after. Yeah, it was a little community they called Shrewsbury, you know, just like they called Harryhann and Kenner up there. Shrewsbury was a little development there or something. And then people lived out there though.
Would you ride the streetcars just to take a ride?

Well sometimes in those days, yeah, it was quite a deal. Amusement? Yeah, like I said, people would take that ride out the Spanish Fort just to, you know, go take a streetcar ride all the way out from Canal Street in town all the way out to the west.
How long would it take to get from Canal Street up to the Spanish Fort?

Oh, I imagine it would take about 45 minutes, I imagine, you know. You know, when we used to... Maybe an hour even, you know, because they used to stop, they used to make stops, you know, you know. They didn't make every stop at the streetcars. They stopped at the main at the section. If they were filled up, they didn't stop. I don't think they remember that.

When my mother would talk to me when I was a little boy, she'd say, Oh, well when we went for a ride, that was a big thing just to go for a ride. Well, that's right, yeah. You know, and people were easily amused, you know. They didn't have anything to do.
Just to look at... They didn't have TV. They didn't have radio. They didn't TV, like that. If you go out on a Saturday and take a ride out to the lake, I mean, it was a big deal.
Yeah.

All the young people used to go out there more or less, and there was dancing out there. There used to be a... I remember the old tuxedo band used to play out the tarantinas out there. Oh yeah? Tarantinas, yeah. Tarantinas, yeah. I think they had a band out there.
Yeah, that was Ridgely and Solestamp's tuxedo band.
And I'll tell you, they played out there too. They had a dance floor out there too. I mean, Bix, not Bix, Bias Dauphin. Yeah. Bias Dauphin used to play out there.
Did you ever go to the Tokyo Gardens, do I think?
No, I didn't go there. Is that the name of the place that they had? It was a dance place. Was that the name of the place? Maybe that's the name of the place?
I think they had a wire fence and everything?
Yeah, I guess it must have been the place. You know Tony Schreiner?
Tony Schreiner, no.
He plays drums now.
He told me about going out there and he'd climb up on the fence.

Maybe it was a board fence, yeah. Well maybe that's the name of the fence. I didn't know because I didn't, see I'm talking about when I was, well quite young, I mean 12 or 13, you know, my family would go out there sometimes. My cousin and I, they'd take my cousin and me and go out to make this. We moved out here, my father bought an old Dodge. I remember we used to ride out there in the car then.
Oh yeah.
One of them old Dodgers.
Yeah, Steve Lloyd Canna.
Oh Steve Lloyd Canna, yeah. I remember Steve Lloyd Canna. I think of some of his names.
Well I know you would have gone for a while. What about bands like Schilling? Did you know Hacker Schilling then?
Yeah I knew the old man, yeah I knew him. And I worked with his son George at one job there and I knew George for years, like later on I used to lead him down in the union and stuff like that.
And Fisher, Johnny Fisher, did you know him? Johnny Fisher?
Well Johnny Fisher, is that the Johnny Fisher that came from New York that you're talking about?
The clarinet play. Oh no, no, no.
He still lives down on North Park.
I know Burgundy now. Burgundy, I think. No, I don't think I knew him. He played clarinet? He played clarinet.
His real name was Phillips.
There was a Johnny Fisher, a trumpet player, around New York.

He played pretty good trumpet. He played with some pretty good band but he was on the blues tour a little bit. Well he came down here later and then he went to the Gulf Coast. Well I don't know where he is. But he and Jack Miranda. You knew John the Fisher that I'm talking about? Yeah, with Jack Miranda and all those guys down here. I knew him in New York for years. Who was he with in New York? I don't know, he played different bands. But like I say, he's hit the blues pretty good a lot of times and he'd lose out on
jobs.

He could get to live in a little bit on a prof bamboo when he could play. I mean, not that I drink myself but they drink all day long and all night too. I'm a night drinker, I don't drink anything at night.
Well you don't drink in your sleep.

No, I'm late now, I have trouble going to sleep, but I have to take a few drinks and try to knock myself out to go to sleep. I'm not doing enough I guess, you know. Not enough exercise, I'm getting enough exercise, I work over there and I'll go out in the yard, but I'm not having enough mental exercise I guess or something, you know, and I can't
sleep.

You don't pay much now, then. Well I'm just on a boat now. I worked, two weeks ago I worked at the, at the, at the, at the Princeville Club, with his violin players Thursday and Friday, you know. About two months ago I worked about five weeks up there, five Thursdays and Friday, you know. What violin player is then? Uh, Baker, Tommy Baker. Oh, he's still in town? Well he was in town, he's gone away again now, he's gone on a summer job. Oh yeah? See when he came in town, he got the job at the Princeville Club Thursday and Friday, and I worked with him at Lothar's and I worked with him at Benham's, you know. Yeah. Well Lothar's has changed the name now.
Yeah, he changed the name.
And he still plays there some time? No, he hasn't played with the new owners, I don't know, he knows them I guess but they didn't put my music in. Yeah.
You played at the Princeville Club with him?
Yeah, I played at the Princeville Club recently, yeah.
One of the table captains at Lothar's is a, well it's not, that's not the name of it anymore. No. I don't know about that. Lothar's has got a new name.
Yeah, well I don't know the new name.

One of the new guys, one of the guys there is a guitarist himself. Oh yeah? You ought to meet him. I think he plays rock or something. But you ought to meet him and talk to him about the chorus and stuff. He might work into something. Anyway, you know I heard a violin play at Brenham's and the guy couldn't play a melody. He was holding on a job at Brenham's. At Brenham's? Yeah. And he couldn't. Do you have a band there now? Oh, this is, I don't know, about a year or so ago. But honestly, he must have been a sub for the night or something.

Well I worked at Brenham's Four once with this Baker guy, and Baker, he plays a lot of violin but he trues you sometimes, you know. Well he's playing ad lib stuff, you know. He plays off time. He plays off time. I know I work with him too. You work with him? Well then you know what I'm talking about. He has no fearful rhythm. I work with him at Lothar too. You know you can play ad lib but still you can play in rhythm, you know what I mean? But he plays-
He can't play in rhythm once he starts trying to live.
Oh he can't, he's hard to work with. I'm one of the few guys that I put up with a lot of stuff working with. But I like to play and it was the only thing I know.
Yeah I worked with him too there at Lothars for a while. You did?
What were you playing?
Guitar? It was piano and guitar. We'd sit down and play for a while and then we'd walk around and pick up the guitar.
But he's hard to work with I tell you. No sense of meter at all.
No. He plays a lot of tunes that you never know.

But he's got a lot of technique though. Yeah. And he knows a lot of tunes and he knows different Greek tunes and stuff and Hungarian stuff. A lot of times he tries to get me to learn the Hungarian stuff but he's faking them himself. He's not playing them right I know. You know what I mean? He's trying to tell me, he always plays like an exercise. It sounds Hungarian style, you know what I mean? But it's not maybe the authentic thing. You know what I mean? No, no. Now when he plays two guitars, I play with Bobrovsky and Bobrovsky plays it right. He plays at the symphony. I mean I worked at Arnold's for about ten years with Bobrovsky on the violin and Gaspar on the card and Bobrovsky plays just another thing on the ground but when he plays a note it sounds like a million dollars because he's got intonation so fine and he plays real good. But he played like two guitars and charters, he'd play them right. When I try to play with this fella, I can't do it with him. He fouls me off. I mean I have to try to foul him but I mean he'd get you all fouled up.
Yeah, that's the way it is. A lot of people like that.

Even a Viennese thing, they try to play, play some of the Viennese waltzes. He plays and he gets all off mute and stuff. I play him with Bobrovsky, he's playing him everything is right, you know, right on the beat.
They got a little group playing there at the German restaurant at Karls. At Karls? Yeah, I was there one night at the Accordion and violin.

Yeah, at Ken Artin. Well he plays fine violin, he's a good all around violin player, Ken. How often do they work there? I think it's been cut down to one night now. They won't work in two nights but I think they cut down to one night. But Ken plays a good all around violin. He's one of the best violin player in town for all around work. He can play a little jazz too, but he knows a lot of tunes and plays good straight violin tunes.
That accordion player that plays with Paul Crawford, you know how you call it, he plays that? Oh yeah, Matt. He plays that too?
He used to. Oh yeah, I didn't know that.
Matt plays good.
He's a nice star. Yeah.

I worked with him when he first started to play and he was, you know, well he just had to experience it. I played a job at the moment, he was just a kid. I played some spot grabber and he'd come on and I just met him. I knew his father. Oh he played too, his father? His father played saxophone, he propelled you.
Oh yeah? Yeah, he played for years. In fact he was on a boat his parents said. He comes on a boat, whatever you want to work he comes on a boat.

What's his father's name? Wait, the son's name Matt, what's his name? Well I can't think of the last name either. I'm tired. That's right. Oh yeah. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.

I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I'm tired. I like that funny. I can't do it. I got stranded in Hammond and I got turned upside down. You know how you get in a place and you can't get any sleep and everything? Yeah. You've had that happen to you when you're on the road. Oh yeah. You can't think straight. Alright. Did you ever see any funerals playing with a brass band and all that?

I've seen them years ago. I never played much. You know. When I lived down the quarter there you'd see them every once in a while. You'd see them all over. Jack Lane and Johnny Lawler used to tell me about playing.
Yeah. You know you must have known Johnny Lawler when you were a little boy because he was a footer.
Yeah.
You know who I'm talking about. The trumpet player. The trumpet player, yeah. Yeah, I'm a player too. I think he was in the French market then.

There were a lot of guys that, well I knew Larry Shields and Harry Shields both of me. And I met some of the original bands, what was Tony Spargo, did he just recently Dialogue or something? Yeah. Yeah. What was his real name, I can't think of it now. Spargo. Yeah, some kind of name, but I know his name was Spargo. But when I first went to New York, he was up there yet. And there was a trombone player, Edwards, who was up in New York. He was still there then? He was still in New York when I went to New York, yeah. He was doing my solo newspaper. Yeah, he's a good trombone.
Good trombone, yeah.
I used to meet him, I used to see him all the time around 50 seconds. You wouldn't get any words? No. What time? I don't know.
But he didn't play the right style?

He didn't play the right style. He was too old-timey. Yeah. He could still play. Yeah, but still it was one of those things around that time, I remember I used to see him almost every night around 50 seconds, he was selling newspapers. Really?
Yeah.

Flo Bernard used to stop and talk to him all the time. Spargo was doing, Spargo got into a lot of other things besides, Spargo played up there yet, but he got into some other things too, I don't know what he was doing, something else, but you know. But Edwards didn't do it, but he didn't sell papers and go in there.
Yeah, well Larry was up there then too. Larry was up there.
Was Larry working with anybody then? I guess he did, but I can't recall where he was at. He was not with any well-known men.
He used to play poker with Hank, come in up there then. Hank would tell me about the poker game.

Well Hank, I remember Hank in New York, I was living with George Horton and the Common Massarin Brothers used to come around. Al? Al, yeah. We had a little apartment there, I think it was on 49th Street. I remember when Hank first came to New York, he'd put up there, he had the North and Mississippi Republic of the apartment. He was down there almost twenty years now, didn't he? Something like that. I told you about one day my daughter came home, my daughter went to Junior High at Burgos, and she came home and she said, my teacher, Miss Komen, I said, who did you say? I said, Miss Komen, how do you spell that? And she told me, I said, do you know, why not if I wasn't a musician? And she was up with Hank's wife. I didn't know she was beating through.
Well listen, when you first went to New York, what band was that you played with? You said at this dancing place?

Oh there was no name of the band, it was just Harry King's band up in the dance hall, you know what I mean? And then later on, like I said, I went to work in the speakeasies for a while, and then after the crash came, the speakeasies got kind of bad, and I got a chance to go to White Plains, you see. I worked at a new group, a nice little band up there, a guy from New York to come and sit in, and they used to listen to Louis records, between sets all the time, they'd hear the record players, all the guys were crazy, they bought arms from them, even then. I mean that's weird back in 29 probably, 29 or early 30. What's it John? The name of the place was called The Farm. The Farm, it was a roadhouse, a restaurant and dancing place, up in Westchester County, White Plains. And there was two brothers, one had a place up on the hill called Uncle Bill's Place, and the other had a place called The Farm. It was built like a log cabin. It was beautiful. I mean he did a terrific business on it. Man, on the weekend, he'd packed that place. He'd get all the cloth and grunts would come up in the air, see, you know, dancing. And people danced plenty in those days. I'll tell you who used to come in, Archie Bly used to come in and bring us some arrangements, when Archie Bly was making arrangements. I played the manuscript on Peanut Thunder before we put it out, you know. He used to try it over, you know, run it over and see, you know. He lived up there, put it down there. He used to make some other tunes for us to play up there too. And what was the band? Who was the band?
Who was the band? There was no name.

The drummer was the leader but there was no name to the band. But like I said, I'll tell you who played in the band, Henry Ross, Hank Ross, do you ever heard of him? He got to be a very good tenor man around New York. And what he was doing just a few years ago when Perry Comer had the show, he was the music coordinator on the Perry Comer show. Yeah, I've heard of him but I can't remember. And then Hank Ross was playing tenor and his brother, his brother named Henry, no Henry and I can't think of his brother's name, not George, no, Benny, Benny Ross. There were two brothers, he played alto and Hank played tenor. And we had another alto player, Joe Denton, he went to Praud, I think he died seven years ago. Joe Denton, I used to ride up there with him and I'd meet him in the Bronx and he'd commute back and forth with the white man, you know, he'd pull out a good stick of tea and move around and drive up to that school. Was that dangerous, riding like that? Yeah. I didn't do it, but he used to. And then we had a drummer, the drummer's name was Ralph Wagner, he was the leader of the band, it was his band, see. But it was more or less a cooperative deal, I mean everybody got the same money, it was his job. Ralph what? Ralph Wagner was his name. I just never heard of these guys. No, he didn't make no name of the band. He didn't make no name for himself, but he worked up in White Plains quite a few years before I went up there. He was up there, he was a half man in the woods. And I'll tell you who worked up on the hill, I remember what up there, Harry and Phillip and what's his name, Harry and Phillip and Ozzie Nelson, was playing at the brother's place up on the hill. Harry Nelson with his college board and he had the band up on the hill there. And Harry Kellett used to sing with the band up there. And we had the other band up there, Tony Sacco played trumpet. Before Tony Sacco there was another fellow who played trumpet. Sacco played trumpet for a while and there was a fellow named Rusty Jones, he was from the Midwest, and he played trombone. We had a girl piano player called Mike. We used to call her Mike. She wasn't a soloist either, but she played good combination piano. And he played with him.
Well you went on that show and you came back here, I got confused now, you played at the Beverly Gardens.
That's the only job I had in New Orleans before I went to the Harrow Office when I went to the Stairway 10 years.
Were you there at the Beverly Gardens a while?

About three months or something like that. And whose band was that one? I don't know who was the leader of the band here. It was like I tell you, Dela Roe on piano and Bonnie Potter on bass, George Shilling, and Paul Piquet, and I can't think of the dumbest name from them. I don't know who actually was the leader of the band, but it was Dela Roe and Ben the Piano player and the big job I'm not sure.
Well don't worry about it. I just can't get these things straight.
Like I said, that was the only job I worked in New Orleans and then I went away until I came back in 76.
What sort of rhythm did they like then on banjo? Did they want you to play?
They wanted this straight sort of forward accent on that beat. You'd accent how? Not a real definite accent, but just a little... Accent the afterbeat level?
Yeah, it would be an afterbeat level. Yeah. Well that's giving you a nice little swing then. I'm sure there wasn't...

There was a lot of, not a lot of band here, but there were some band of players around New York, so you could come up to a place and they'd dance all the players sometimes. I can't believe, some fellow was a teacher. I can't believe, some fellow was a teacher. I can't believe, some of the same. But the banjo era, that didn't last too long in New York. I got there in 26 and I worked in a dance hall in 27 and 28 and then in 29 I had to swing the guitar. And the banjo just went out completely and I forgot about it. I had a banjo stolen in a dance hall for me. Before I left here I bought a vega banjo from Howard Voorhees and I told them when I get my first job I'll buy a banjo. When I get a job in a tent show I went and bought a $100 vega from Howard Voorhees. I know him for years. And then when I got in New York I bought a $400 tom on banjo. I had one more payment to make on it and then somebody had their eye on a gold banjo. They had a room full of instruments up there, flutes and clannets and all, and all they took was a banjo. And I got so mad I went out and bought another one just like. And then when I bought the other one, I got it paid off there just when I was down. Then I bought a Morton guitar first and then I got a Gibson. And then I changed that performance. I used to go down to that performance factory, most of the guys would go down to the factory and they used to loan this instruments to try them out and see, they were trying to get an idea what the fellas wanted in a guitar, for playing in the band. And Gibson made the only guitar at the time but that performance was coming up and I used to go, I used to know the owner of Old Man's Stapopola was a Greek, he made the upper phone guitar epic. That's where they get the name of the phone from. Epi Stapopola. And he died and the brother took it over, Arceus took it over and then the company kind of went down after that. But all the time that I was in New York, Epi was the one that they had at the company. And like I said, we used to go down to the factory and they let us take instruments out and try them out for a few days and see them and come back and give our criticism of what we thought, you know, if it felt too heavy or the top seemed like it was too thick or something like that. They were trying to get a pretty good deal, you know, which they did. I got an upper phone and I'm using Epi. Were they using Epi?
Go ahead.
How long have you had this one?
I bought that in 1943 when I was in Detroit.

That's a good deal. Yeah. But I got some work done on it but the upper phone, a Japanese phone bought them out now but I'm going to go, I plan on going to Michigan this summer. My wife, got a sister, lives up in Detroit, Pontiac. If I go up there, I'm going to take it up there with them and go over to Kalamazoo with it. I want them to fix the neck for me, neck walk down. I could send it to them, I could send it one time to them but it takes so long when they send it up there. I want to see, besides I'd like to see the factory, I want to see the key. I'm going to try to make a trip to Kalamazoo and take the guitar right there.
Were people using F-hole guitars or round holes or what then?

Well the first guitar I bought was a Martin, but I wish I had kept it, but I traded it in on a Gibson, but I wish I had kept it doing things, because I'd like to have a round hole guitar too. It's a compliment, but the drum player is pretty good for that kind of work. It's better for sure. And the Gibson had what they called a Gibson L5, that could be the guitar, the old one, you know, with the Ebony bridge and all, but then they improved on the Gibson too. You can't change the model of it so it doesn't.
Do you think the guitars they make today are as good as the old ones?

Oh yeah, I think they're pretty good. Well like the guitars that you've got now, you can't buy a guitar like that. No, I know you can't. You can't buy them anymore. You can't buy them, but it takes a long time to get them. If you try to buy a Gibson L5, that might take you over a year before you get the ground thing, you know? You have to order it. They have to put a special order in for it. They don't make it. Like a Johnny Smith model, they have to maybe wait over a year for the ground thing.
Johnny Smith model?
Yeah, Johnny Smith got a model, Johnny Smith guitar model. Yeah.
I've been wanting to get a guitar similar to yours, but you're not supposed to see them anyway.
What kind of guitars you got there?
Well I have just a cheap Gibson guitar, you know, Lady model. I don't like it.
You had a cheap one?
Yeah. It didn't sound too bad at all. It's okay, but I like to have one, something like your guitar, but you can't see them anyway. I've been looking around.
No, the only place you could find, you see them advertising the musicians thing, but they want a lot of money for someone.
Yeah, I know. See the reason I would like to have a guitar like that, I like to have a guitar that you can use both acoustic and... That's what I kept it.
Most of the amplifier guitars, they're no good in the acoustic.
They're completely dead. No good, no. That's why...
That's what mine is.
Mine is dead acoustic.

Because most of the work I did was rhythm work, and a lot of times I didn't use the amplifier much, or very little, you know what I mean? And so I didn't want to buy one of them electric guitars, because I... They're no good then. I started using it with Sharky, but I wasn't using it too much with Sharky, because I played strictly Dixieland most of the time, you know.
You didn't want to use the amplifier?

No, but I used it in the hotel with Sharky, because I had bought this Hawaiian guitar, and I was fooling around with the amplifier, and I used the amplifier mostly for the Hawaiian guitar. What was that when you got an amplifier? That was 39 I think, when I started to use the thing. And these fellas picked me up about 1940, they're the one who got me using electric more. Yeah. When I joined them, they got me using them.
How long, when did they start? They had, they started having amplifiers before then? A little bit before that, yeah.
About 38?
They had acoustical amplifiers and all kinds of new deals, you know.

But there wasn't too much amplification before that, I don't know when it actually started, but like I said, I started using the Hawaiian thing, I bought that Hawaiian guitar, and I used the amplifier for that, but I didn't use it on the Spanish guitar, I didn't even have the almond pick up yet now, you see. And then when I went with this group at the hotel, in fact I never stood up and played guitar at the moment. He's the one who made the strap, I got the strap and he made it for me. He didn't make it, but he told me how to make the strap out of an accordion deal and go to a belt maker and get a big thick belt and have a sword and all that, you know what I mean? I made that thing in 1940, still on the guitar.
Oh yeah?

The same strap? The same strap. And I went to a saddle maker and got a piece of belt in, you know, and had him sort of a cordial strap on it and kind of put it on the end. But he's the one, this fellow that played bass and drums at this house, he did a lot of work with groups that stood up and played, you know, that stood up and played at that time, and it was fairly new in some locations, down here you didn't see much bands standing up and play, you know, it was more of a way to sit down and play before that, you know, and then, but when I went with them, I got used to standing up and that's when I thought he was an amplifier.
Did you ever see anybody put a microphone in front of the guitar?
Oh yeah, they used to do that, they would show me off when the guitars first came out too.
Turn it over now for the second. Yeah. Is that about Van Epps? Well, Van Epps used to get up on the mic when he took solos or something like that,
when he made recordings and all, he didn't know how many of you used the mic. Rather than to have an amplifier.
Huh? He used that instead of having an amplifier.

Instead of having an amplifier, yeah. Well, the amplifier was fairly new yet. I mean, I didn't use much amplification on the guitar, I didn't have the pickups on the guitar, they used to get up closer to my guitar. Well, did it sound like a guitar? It sounded more like a guitar than with the amplifier. The amplifier changes the tone of the guitar. Yeah, right.
It changes the entire quality of the guitar. Yeah.

more of a guitar tone on it than a modern guitar. I got a Gibson amplifier, I bought it there, a big double speaker, and it's the one I've been using for, well I guess the thing is, I must have it over ten years now. It's heavy, I'll tell you that. It's heavy, oh, that's one of the ones heavy. I helped you carry it one time. Yeah, I know it. But it's pretty good, I haven't had no trouble with it. I don't have trouble with it. I don't have trouble with it.

It's more like a guitar than with the amplifier. It's more like a guitar than with the amplifier. The amplifier changes the tone of the guitar. Yeah. It changes the entire quality of the guitar. Yeah. It changes the entire quality of the guitar.

Yeah. That's why it's best to have the guitar you got. The old style guitar you got more of a guitar tone on it than a modern guitar. I got a Gibson amplifier, I bought it there, a big double speaker, and it's a guitar. I'm not saying it's heavy for over ten years now. It's heavy, I'll tell you that. It's heavy, oh, that's one of the ones heavy.
I helped you carry it one time. Yeah, I know it.

But it's pretty good. I don't have any trouble with it. I'll tell you what I sent for, something new, it must be a booster. I've seen an advertisement, a musician thing in New York, they've got little things that you're supposed to plug in. They don't tell you much in the advertisement, but I guess you plug it in the amplifier and then plug the instrument in. I'm not buying it for volume. And I sent for the thing, and they got a lot of stuff. My check went through the bank and they cashed my check in, and the check came back in my statement. I never received a thing. I wrote them a letter last night. I told them I got the check here, and if they want it, I'll send them a 40-sided copy of the check if they want it. But I told them the check is made out. They endorsed the check. They cashed it, but they never sent you this thing. The reason I wrote them to them about it, they got an amplifier, a portable amplifier they put them out. A small lamp, it doesn't weigh very much, it's supposed to be very powerful. It doesn't have any tubes. It works in the battery. It works in the battery, too. I see. Yeah, and it's supposed to last a pretty good while, and I want to find out more about
it.
It would be nice for you. If it's any good, yeah. This thing is so hard to carry around. It's killing it.
Well you know, Floyd Smith, I don't know if you ever heard him, you used to do with Andy
Kirk? Yeah.

He had some deal with that electricity where he would amplify the sound of his guitar, and I never have seen it. But you know they would have resonators and different things. Yeah, well he used to play fine guitar, boy.

I used to listen to him all the time. He'd come true nice, just to write a note, you know, pretty nice. But they had all kind of deals, which I don't know much about on guitar. You know, to bring the tone out. I'll tell you something that happened to me in Detroit, after this job that I did, I broke up at the old Wayne Club in Detroit, so I stayed in Detroit that summer, a couple of the guys I met in Detroit talked me into going on a boat, on the great boat up the Mackinac Island, on the Great Lakes cruise boats, you know, they used to make two trips a week, see on a Friday they'd leave and come back on a Monday morning, go on Monday evening, stay on a Friday. And I worked with a group on about five pieces. Fred Day was the leader, he's a Detroit local, he's on the board up there now. He had the job and then we had no bass. We had trumpet, sax, piano, drums and guitars. And I missed the bass so much, on some tunes like Lady Be Good or something like those up tunes, you know, I missed the bass and I picked the bass on the guitar. I put my volume up and just picked on the bass and made like boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, you know, this like a bass. You know, that's before actually basses ever came out. And I worked around Detroit and a couple of clubs around there, another group, four-piece group at Aquarian and Clownet and stuff. And the same thing, we had no bass there and I missed the bass so much in a group like that. Instead of playing guitar, I played bass on some tunes, you know, and guys would come in the place and say, where's the bass? I said, are you looking for the bass that couldn't find the bass? Before electric basses came out. I could have made a million bucks probably, but I'd have been smart.
Well of course you never knew that rock and roll was that? No. Did you ever know Mez Mezroy around here?

Yeah, I got a record I made with him. Oh yeah? Yeah. I got the record here. The only record I got was an old Brunswick record. And I played it some time ago but I don't know if it got wonk, it don't sound so good no more.
Teddy Wilson was on it. Was he any good then? Yeah, he played fine.
When he first came to New York, he was one of his first, I guess one of his first record dates. I got the record here. I like to hear a good machine sometime but I think-

Well, we'll, we have to come and get all this stuff together and we can all go over there. Tulane and maybe we can weight the needle down or something and we might take that. Yeah, I think so might take it, yeah.
You want to try it sometime? Yeah. You want to do it any time you want.

I'm pretty sure.

Yeah, Floyd O'Brien is who played trombone. I always get that record mixed up with the ones I made with Wingy because it was a mixed band. They both were mixed bands. I was playing and I'd get them mixed up sometimes. Yeah, Floyd O'Brien made that record.

Well they made records together. But did they play in clubs? I played a radio broadcast with Chick Webb one time, at the radio station with Chick Webb, the short punch back drum, you know, stand up and play. He played a mess of drums, boy.

Did you know the guys in Louis Russell's band? No, I didn't get them all. About half of them from New Orleans, you know? Well they were, but I didn't get the, I wasn't that long of a band. Did you know, what did Maher's play like is what I'm trying to say?

Oh I can't, he played pretty good, but I can't remember the styles of them, so I've got to listen to the record myself to bring back the memory, I really can't tell. What about Pop Foster, was he any good? Well that's what Pop Foster made the record with, let's see, yeah with Mez, yeah he was on the record day, Pop Foster that's right.

That's right, I mean, I. That's right. I mean, I. That's right. That's right. Eddie Wilson. Who, did they do, did you have arrangements in the band? Yeah, there was, somebody made arrangements for me. I don't know who he was, maybe, you know. I wish the dumb machine was kind of a fit for him.
Did you know a guy named Ben Gussick or Cusick or something?
Yeah, a drummer?

And there was Ham Russon too.
Babe, and then his brother played piano, Jacky Russon played piano.

Yeah. Well it must have been Freddie then, I was trying to think of his first name.

It wasn't a bass player, it must have been Freddie that had just come up to the new, when I lived with Sharky, he used to get the trumpet all the time, yeah. Freddie must have been that. Yeah. I got to New York and he'd say, meet Sunshine, my real name. And a lot of guys in the world didn't even know my real name. I knew a lot of people up there but none of them knew my real name.

It was late too, New Year's Eve, we went up there. Somewhere up in the Bronx, we went up there. I remember growing up there with Sharky and all of us, and we really had a big one. All you wanted to eat and drink.
